Chapter 4: Sacrifice and Self-Denial as the Heart of Faith
You know, a lot of people think faith is all about comfort—finding peace, security, maybe even happiness. But if you’ve ever really tried to live out your beliefs, you already know... it’s rarely that simple.
True faith asks for more. It calls us to let go, to give up, to sacrifice in ways that can feel uncomfortable or even risky.
Picture someone who’s always put themselves first. Then, out of the blue, a friend needs help—real help—even though it means missing out on something they care about. The choice might not be dramatic, but it’s real. It’s a small act of letting go... a kind of quiet self-denial, for someone else’s sake.
That’s really the core of sacrifice and self-denial. It isn’t about making a big scene or showing off. It’s about those everyday moments—the simple, often unnoticed choices to put someone else first. They might slip by without applause, but honestly, these are the moments that shape a life of faith.
Sacrifice isn’t about trying to earn favor or prove how good you are. It’s a response to love—a willingness to keep going, even when it’s tough. Think of a parent working long hours, setting aside their own dreams just so their kids can have a better life. The sacrifice is real, no doubt. But the joy that comes from seeing their family thrive? That’s real, too.
Self-denial doesn’t mean you stop caring about yourself or ignore your needs. It means you realize life is bigger than your own wants. You start to find meaning in serving others, in giving instead of always taking. And as you do, those choices begin to build a sense of purpose and fulfillment—something comfort alone just can’t give.
In a world that’s always shouting about self-fulfillment, choosing sacrifice and self-denial might seem strange... maybe even foolish. But if you’ve ever walked this path, you know the truth: it leads to a deeper joy—a joy you only find when you live for something greater than yourself.
